# Digital Signatures

Sign with the private key, verify with the public one — the reverse of encryption's key usage, and the
source of three properties encryption alone does not provide. Labs 06 and 07 of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]] build and then attack them.

## The three guarantees

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Authentication** | the holder of the private key produced this |
| **Integrity** | the data has not changed since it was signed |
| **Non-repudiation** | the signer cannot later disown the signature |

Non-repudiation is the one that has no symmetric-key equivalent. A MAC gives authentication and
integrity, but both parties hold the same key, so either could have produced the tag — neither can
prove the other did. That asymmetry of *evidence* is why signatures underpin contracts, code signing,
certificate issuance and blockchain transactions.

## The construction, and where the hash sits

Three algorithms: key generation, signing, verification. Signing does **not** encrypt the document —
it hashes the document and applies the private-key operation to the digest. The hash is not a
performance optimisation bolted on; it is structural, and it relocates the entire security of the
scheme onto the hash function.

Which sets up the attack.

## The hash-collision attack on a signature

If two different documents hash to the same value, **one signature is valid for both.** Get a
signature on the innocuous document, attach it to the malicious one, and verification passes — the
verifier only ever sees the digest. Lab 06 runs exactly this demonstration in [[cryptool]]: construct
a collision, sign one preimage, verify against the other.

The consequence for practice: MD5 and SHA-1 are unusable for signatures regardless of how carefully
the signing key is managed. Collision resistance — not preimage resistance — is the property that
matters here, and it is the one that falls first.

## Verification failure modes

The repository's own selected screenshot for lab 07 is the sign/verify page, and the reason given for
choosing it is that the *failures* are more instructive than the success: verifying against the wrong
public key, and omitting the signature argument, fail in different ways. A verification step that can
only be observed succeeding teaches nothing about what a real rejection looks like — the same instinct
as [[document-the-failure-mode-next-to-the-fix]].

The page that would have been the obvious illustration was deliberately not used, because it printed a
private key — see [[omit-rsa-private-key-screenshot]].

## The algorithms

RSA (sign with the private exponent), DSA, and the elliptic-curve family ECDSA/EdDSA. The lab
exercises RSA signing through [[openssl]] `dgst` and OpenPGP signing through GnuPG, plus HMAC as the
symmetric counterpart. The attack models enumerated are key-only, known-message and adaptive
chosen-message — the same taxonomy [[cryptanalysis-by-measurement]] uses for ciphers, applied to a
signature scheme.

## Signatures are only as good as the binding

A valid signature proves a private key was used. It says nothing about **whose** key that was. The
binding from key to identity is external to the signature entirely, which is what
[[public-key-infrastructure]] provides — and why signature verification in TLS or in a package manager
is always chained to a trust store rather than terminating at a single key.
